title: Richter's Question
statement_text: Given an integer $n \geq 5$ and a graph $G$ with crossing number at least $\operatorname{cr}(K_n)$, does it follow that the crossing number of its cone $CG$ is at least $\operatorname{cr}(K_{n+1})$?
context_text: Richter posed this question during the Crossing Numbers Workshop in 2013 in an attempt to understand Albertson's conjecture. Simple examples show the two values can differ arbitrarily, but the question asks whether the cone's crossing number is always at least as large as the next complete-graph threshold.
paper_contribution: Shows the answer is positive for $n = 5$ via Kuratowski's theorem, but negative for $n = 6$ by exhibiting a graph with crossing number 3 whose cone has crossing number at most 6, strictly less than $\operatorname{cr}(K_7) = 9$.
paper_title: The crossing number of the cone of a graph

title: Problem 1
statement_text: For each $k \geq 0$, find the smallest integer $f(k)$ for which there is a graph $G$ with crossing number at least $k$ and its cone has $\operatorname{cr}(CG) = f(k)$.
context_text: Graphs may have multiple edges but no loops (simple graphs have no multiple edges); $\operatorname{cr}(G)$ is the crossing number. The cone $CG$ of a graph $G$ is obtained from $G$ by adding a new vertex (the apex) adjacent to every vertex of $G$. Richter asked whether $\operatorname{cr}(G)\ge\operatorname{cr}(K_n)$ implies $\operatorname{cr}(CG)\ge\operatorname{cr}(K_{n+1})$ for $n\ge5$; this holds for $n=5$ but fails for $n=6$: the authors exhibit a graph with crossing number 3 whose cone has crossing number at most 6, less than $\operatorname{cr}(K_7)=9$. This motivates asking for the minimum possible crossing number of a cone over all graphs of a given crossing number; equivalently, $f(k)$ is the largest integer such that every graph with $\operatorname{cr}(G)\ge k$ satisfies $\operatorname{cr}(CG)\ge f(k)$. The paper proves $f(k)=k+\Theta(\sqrt{k})$ when multiple edges are allowed. For simple graphs the analogous function $f_s(k)$ satisfies $f_s(1)=3$, $f_s(2)=5$, $f_s(3)=6$, $f_s(4)=8$, $f_s(5)=10$ and $f_s(k)=k+o(k)$.

title: Problem 4
statement_text: Given a 1-page drawing of a graph $G$ with $k$ crossings, find an upper bound on the number of crossings of an optimal 2-page drawing of $G$ while having the order of vertices of $G$ on the spine unchanged.
context_text: For $k\ge1$, a $k$-page book consists of $k$ half-planes sharing their boundary line (the spine); a $k$-page drawing places the vertices on the spine and draws each edge inside one page. A 1-page drawing is equivalent to a drawing in which all vertices lie on the outer face. An optimal 2-page drawing here means one minimizing the number of crossings among 2-page drawings with the same cyclic order of the vertices on the spine. Equivalently: if $G$ is drawn in the plane with all vertices on the outer face and $k$ crossings, what is the most efficient way to redraw some edges in the outer face to reduce crossings? The circle graph $C_D$ of a 1-page drawing $D$ has the edges of $G$ as vertices, two being adjacent if they cross in $D$; choosing a 2-page drawing amounts to a bipartition of $V(C_D)$, so minimizing crossings is a max-cut problem on $C_D$. Using Edwards' max-cut bound, the authors show that some edges can be moved to a second page to obtain at most $\frac{1}{2}k-\sqrt{\frac{1}{8}k+\frac{1}{64}}+\frac{1}{8}$ crossings, which is a partial answer. The question is closely related to the crossing number of the cone of $G$ (the graph obtained by adding a vertex adjacent to all vertices), since the face containing the apex in a drawing of the cone yields 1-page drawings. A related notion is Kainen's outerplanar crossing number.

title: Conjecture on $f_s(k)$ asymptotics
context_text: Graphs may have multiple edges but no loops (simple graphs have no multiple edges); $\operatorname{cr}(G)$ is the crossing number. The cone $CG$ of a graph $G$ is obtained from $G$ by adding a new vertex (the apex) adjacent to every vertex of $G$. $f_s(k)$ is the smallest integer for which there is a simple graph $G$ with $\operatorname{cr}(G)\ge k$ and $\operatorname{cr}(CG)=f_s(k)$; the authors write $\phi_s(k)=f_s(k)-k$, so the conjecture states $\phi_s(k)=\sqrt{2}\,k^{3/4}(1+o(1))$. The small values $f_s(1)=3$, $f_s(2)=5$, $f_s(3)=6$, $f_s(4)=8$, $f_s(5)=10$ might suggest $f_s(k)\ge 2k$, but the authors show $f_s(k)=k+o(k)$. In contrast, for multigraphs the corresponding function satisfies $f(k)=k+\Theta(\sqrt{k})$. As justification, they prove that if the Harary–Hill conjecture holds ($\operatorname{cr}(K_n)=\frac{1}{64}n(n-2)^2(n-4)$ for even $n$ and $\frac{1}{64}(n-1)^2(n-3)^2$ for odd $n$), then $\phi_s(k)\le\sqrt{2}\,k^{3/4}(1+o(1))$, using $G=K_{n-1}\cup K_{n_1}$ for suitable $n,n_1$; they conjecture this gives the precise asymptotics.
notes: Stated as an informal conjecture in running prose without a labelled theorem environment; PDF source — math notation ($\sqrt{2}\,k^{3/4}$) may be partially garbled.
